About the synagogue ruler’s daughter it is written that “when the crowd was put out, Jesus went in, took her hand, and the girl was raised.” Why did he not rather, as with Lazarus, content himself with a word for the girl’s rising, but also took her hand? To show that his body gives life — for it is a body of life. So the union of the Word toward the flesh is rather natural and true, and not, as some say from ignorance, done only in persons, or according to bare praise and will, or mere conjunction.
From John’s Gospel. “Work,” he says, “not for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains into eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for on this one the Father…

title: Exact imprint; life-giving touch; hilasterion in his blood
english: …God has sealed.” The Son of Man has given us the food that remains into eternal life — clearly his flesh; for it is life-giving. Then how is the one who can give life even through his own flesh not God, and like in all things to God the Father? For this I take to be what it means to say he has been sealed by God — “to have been sealed” signifying the exact likeness. For just as if someone presses a gold seal — or one made of another material — into wax, he marks the whole impress of it from the whole, so also God the Father has the characters of his own nature essentially shining in the Son. And this is what it means to say he has been sealed by the Father.

From Luke’s Gospel. Christ raised Lazarus, the synagogue ruler’s little daughter, the widow’s son. Then how is he not life by nature — the one who can terrify death not only by a word but also by the touch of the hand? For it was both fitting and necessary that the body of the life by nature be life-giving.

That he is a hilasterion through faith. From the letter to the Romans. About Christ he says: “Whom God put forward as a hilasterion through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness, because of the passing over of the sins that had happened before in God’s forbearance, toward the demonstration of his righteousness in the present time, so that he might be…

title: Redeemed by his blood; gifts prove God; baptism into his death
english: If Christ could not otherwise become a hilasterion for those under sin and curse and death’s sentence except that blood was going to be poured out “because of the passing over of the sins that had happened before,” how was it not necessary that the Word become flesh — so that by his own blood, clearly that of his own flesh, he might justify all who believe in him?

That we have been redeemed and have obtained reconciliation toward God through his blood. From the first letter to the Corinthians. “From him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that as it is written: Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” So we have been redeemed in Christ and sanctified and have become wise; “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” — that is, from God. Then how is Christ not God — the one who has gifted us wisdom and sanctification and redemption?

That we have been redeemed through the blood of Christ. From Peter’s letter. “Knowing that you were not redeemed with perishable things, silver or gold, from your futile ancestral way of life, but with precious blood as of a lamb without blemish and without spot — Christ.” For we have been redeemed, Christ having given his own body for us. But if he is understood as a common human, how is his blood a match for the life of all? But if the one worthier than all was God in flesh, he would be sufficient for the redemption of the whole world through his own blood — and very reasonably so.

That Christ’s death is saving for the world. From Romans. “God demonstrates his own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us. Much more then, having now been justified in his blood, we will be saved through him from wrath.” And again: “For if, being enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we will be saved in his life.” So if the world could not otherwise be saved except in blood and death taken up usefully and economically “because of the passing over of the sins that had happened before in God’s forbearance,” and we have been saved through Christ — how is the mode of incarnation not necessary for the Word born from God? So that he might justify those who believe in him in his blood, and reconcile them to the Father through the death of his own body, so that we might also live with him.

“Or do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.” If those on earth must somehow be buried with Christ through baptism into his death, so that just as he has been raised from the dead we too might walk in newness of life, as co-buried and co-raised with the one who died and was raised for us —

title: Share flesh and blood; second Adam; curse on the tree
english: Most usefully and of necessity the mystery of the becoming-human has been accomplished: the Word shared flesh and blood, so that to the one said to die fleshly and also to have been raised we might die with him and be raised with him.

“For if we have become grown-together with the likeness of his death, we will also be of the resurrection.” You will understand these things in the same way as the first. “For since through a human comes death, through a human also comes resurrection of the dead; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.” Christ has been named second Adam; and just as the first Adam brought us down into corruption, so also Christ brought us back up into life — not as a bare human who died for us, lest we also remain dead in him, but as God in flesh, having suffered in it humanly, so that when he raised his own temple divinely we might be raised with him.

From Galatians. “Christ bought us out of the curse of the law, becoming a curse for us; for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree — so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.” Look here too: Christ’s death has become saving for the world. For he became a curse for us, enduring a cross and hanging on a tree, so that he might loose the world’s sin, “so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus” — that is, so that the nations might be justified through faith according to the promise given to Abraham, “so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”

title: Law’s curse loosed; blood gathers the far; faith as toward God
english: So when Christ’s death has also loosed the curse in the law, and has procured for the nations Abraham’s blessing — that is, the grace through faith — and has shown us also as sharers of the Holy Spirit, his death would not be understood as that of a common human. Rather one should think that the Word, having become flesh, suffered in flesh for the world, and his suffering became sufficient for the world’s redemption.

From Ephesians. “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far have become near in the blood of Christ; for he himself is our peace, who made both one and loosed the dividing wall of the fence, the enmity in his flesh, having abolished the law of the commandments in decrees.” If Christ’s blood has also made near those who were far because they wandered through the world and continued in godlessness, how is the Word’s becoming-flesh not necessary for those on earth — gathering the divided and making the far kin to God, and creating the two peoples into one new human through his flesh? For he has been given for the redemption of those in sins, and through him he acquired all things for God and Father, and besides this the old law has also been abolished, as faith being above it — clearly the faith in Christ. And if this is true, how is faith above law unless we have believed in Christ as God?

From Hebrews. “Therefore, entering into the world, he says: Sacrifice and offering you did not will, but a body you prepared for me; whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin you did not delight in; then I said: Behold, I have come — in the roll of the book it is written about me — to do, O God, your will.”

title: Only-begotten enters; divine blood; mediator enough for all; impassible yet passible
english: Christ’s suffering has become saving for the world; yet it is necessary to see who the one entering into the world is. For he was outside the world wholly and entirely — since how has he entered into it if he was not outside the world? Therefore, existing by nature above the whole world as Only-begotten God, he has entered into it, having become a part of it — that is, a human — and thus, having offered the sacrifice for us and dedicated himself, he has saved what is under heaven.

“Therefore Jesus also, so that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.” How would a common human’s blood show us holy? But Christ’s blood has sanctified. So it is divine, then, and not simply human; for God was in flesh, cleansing us by his own blood.

From the letter to Timothy. “For there is one God, and one mediator of God and humans, the human Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.” Christ’s death is confessedly saving for the whole world. Yet if he is not God, how would he himself alone suffice to become a ransom for all? But he alone sufficed, dying for all, because he is also above all. So he is God, then — having destroyed the world’s death by the death of his own flesh.

From Peter’s letter. “Because Christ once died concerning sins, a righteous one for unrighteous ones, so that he might bring us to God, put to death in flesh but made alive in spirit; in which also he went and preached to the spirits in prison who once were disobedient.” Many of the holy prophets have been killed, but none of those is said to have died for sins, nor to bring us to God through his own death, nor did anyone preach to the spirits in prison. But Christ has done this, and through him and in him we have been redeemed, and his suffering was saving for the world. So he died for us not as one human among those like us, but as God in flesh, giving his own body as an exchange for the life of all.

“Christ therefore having suffered for us in flesh.” For as Christ being God, the disciple wisely and thoughtfully says he has suffered in flesh, exempting from suffering the ineffable nature, to which suffering is foreign. So he has suffered in his own flesh, though the Word from God is accustomed to have no share in suffering. So Christ is God, then — impassible divinely, but passible according to the flesh.

title: Grain dies into glory; Word’s flesh-suffering; hypostatic union needed
english: …and again: “Jesus answers them saying: The hour has come so that the Son of Man may be glorified; amen, amen, I say to you, unless the grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” And it is not doubtful that the whole world has been saved, Emmanuel having died for it. Yet we say this: how was he glorified by dying? And yet the matter rather has a stigma of weakness — which is why it is also called a despising of shame, having become obedient unto death. But perhaps you will say that he has been glorified through the resurrection. The word holds rightly and is true. Did he then return to life divinely rather than humanly? But I think divinely. So when the Word from God himself is said to suffer in flesh, let us not be ashamed of the suffering; for the end has glory, and this is God-befitting.

That there is one Son of God and Lord, Jesus Christ. From Romans. “I myself with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin. So there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus; for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus freed me from the law of sin and of death. For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of flesh of sin and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to flesh but according to Spirit.” For flesh and Spirit confessedly fight each other… But now in Christ what stands against has been loosed… For God has sent his own Son in the likeness of flesh of sin so that he might condemn sin in the flesh — then how is the Word’s becoming-flesh not exceedingly necessary? For thus sin has also been condemned in our flesh. But if the Word has not become flesh, the things concerning us have remained uncorrected… So we say the Word’s union with the flesh according to hypostasis is necessary — and not only the one in persons and according to will, or a bare conjunction, as some say.

title: Justifier is true God; Word’s own body at the right hand
english: “Who will bring a charge against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies; who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus who died — rather also was raised — who is at God’s right hand, who also intercedes for us.” If Christ justifies by faith, and the one who justifies is God, then Christ is true God. And if he is at God’s right hand, although he has died and been raised, and sits with the Father, then the body is the Word’s own. For thus he sits with the Father with the assumed flesh, as Son by nature even if the Word has become flesh.

“But the righteousness from faith says thus: Do not say in your heart, Who will go up into heaven? — that is, to bring Christ down — or Who will go down into the abyss? — that is, to bring Christ up from the dead. But what does it say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart — that is, the word of faith that we preach — that if you confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved…” If according to what some think Christ is understood as a God-bearing human and has only the union in persons toward the Word from God, why, believing in him as Lord and also confessing his resurrection from the dead, are we justified by the faith toward him? And the faith is clearly done as toward God. Therefore the God-Word’s union according to hypostasis toward the human things is necessary.

title: Belong to the Lord in life and death; incarnation for lordship
english: “For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself; if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord; so whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ died and lived, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.” The blessed Paul has somewhere addressed those from the nations: “But now knowing God — rather being known by God — how do you turn back to the weak and poor elements…?” So through the faith toward Christ we have been redeemed from slavery to the elements, and have been brought to serve the living and true God. And if Christ also died so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living, and we live to him as to the living and true God, how is the economy of becoming-flesh not necessary for the Word from God?

title: After rising, confess Christ from divine excellence; under law as God
english: “And if we have known Christ according to flesh, yet now we no longer know him.” What then does Paul say? Does he deny Christ after the resurrection? Does he not know him raised in flesh and taken up with it into heaven? And who would dare to say that? For thus he also knows him taken up and going to come at the times in the way he has gone up into heaven. How then does he say he does not know Christ according to flesh? Because after the return to life from the dead, it is better to know and confess him not still from the flesh’s measures, but as from divine superiority. For while the economy was not yet fulfilled he was preached according to flesh, so that the Only-begotten might be believed to have become human; but since the mystery has been completed, it is better to confess him from what he is as God than from the having-been-emptied through the flesh. So there is one Christ and Son and Lord.

From Galatians. “But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, become from a woman, become under law, so that he might buy out those under law, so that we might receive the adoption.” As God he became under law so that he might also become brother to those under law; for thus we have received the adoption.

title: Spirit of the Son proves deity; one ascending–descending Lord
english: As God he became under law so that he might also become brother to those under law; for thus we have received the adoption. So if he had not become under law and from a woman, we would not even be brothers to the Lord and God by nature; but since he became so, we have been enriched with what is his. The inspired Paul makes proof of the matter, bringing at once: “And because you are sons, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: Abba, Father.” How then is the Spirit of the one from a woman and under law the Holy Spirit, through whom we also cry Abba, Father, unless Christ is God, being one and Son?

From Ephesians. “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. But to each one of us was given the grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ; therefore it says: Having gone up into height he led captivity captive and gave gifts to humans. Now the ‘He went up’—what is it except that he also went down into the lower parts of the earth? The one who went down is himself also the one who went up above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.” See again how great a word in this shows most clearly and vividly that Christ and Lord is one by an economic union of the Word brought together toward the human; for from both there is one true Son. For how is there one Lord? How one faith? Or how is baptism one? If there were two sons, there would altogether be two lords, a double faith, and baptism would not be one. For into whom have we believed? Or into whose name have we been baptized? But there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism. So it is clear that there is also one Son, even if the Only-begotten is understood as having become as we are. And who at all is the one who went up into height? Or who the one who came down into the lower parts of the earth? Therefore he himself went down humanly—for he let himself down into emptying and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—and went up with the flesh above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.

title: Kenosis and exaltation; Colossians image and firstborn
english: From Philippians. “Let this be minded in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking a slave’s form, becoming in humans’ likeness, and being found in fashion as a human he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death of a cross; therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” Understand how he says that the God-Word, existing in the form and equality of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized. For having being by nature in equality with the Father, he emptied himself, and taking a slave’s form—that is, having become human—and being found as it were in our form, he humbled himself into emptying. And since he also endured the cross itself, it says he is exalted, and that the name above every name has been given him so that every knee should bow and every tongue confess to him. How then does the one in God’s form and equality let himself down into emptying, and after this is said to be exalted? Is not Christ’s mystery most evident? For being God by nature he became human in humiliation and lowliness, and having become as we are, he ascends again into his own glory even with flesh. And being exalted would befit the economy, not rather the Word’s nature itself. So there is one Christ, God in humanity, and with the humanity remaining what he was.

From Colossians. “Giving thanks to the Father who made us fit for the portion of the lot of the saints in the light, who rescued us from the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have the redemption, the forgiveness of sins; who is the image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation, because in him all things were created… and he is before all and all things hold together in him, and he is the head of the body, the church; who is beginning, firstborn from the dead, so that he might become in all things himself first, because in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross…”

title: Image and firstborn from dead; Hebrews heir through flesh
english: See again: he calls him the image of the invisible God, and clearly affirms that thrones and rulers and lordships were created through him, and says that all things are unto him and hold together in him, and that he is the head of the body’s church and firstborn from the dead. Who then is the image of God, the creator of the wholes, if not the Only-begotten Son of God himself? Who also became firstborn from the dead, as having died in his own flesh and not rather in someone else’s. So there is one Christ and Son, God and human together.

From Hebrews. “In many parts and in many ways God, having spoken of old to the fathers in the prophets, in these last days spoke to us in a Son, whom he placed heir of all, through whom he also made the ages.” The Only-begotten Word is believed to be by nature Lord of the wholes with God and Father, yet he is placed heir because he became flesh. For it was said to him, as one who appeared as a human like us for our sake: “Ask of me, and I will give you nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” But he says that through this same God who is heir—because of the human—the ages themselves were also made, the matter referring back to the Word’s seniority. So there is one Christ and Son, the same one God and human together.

title: Radiance sits by own blood; sanctifier and sanctified one Son
english: “Who being the radiance of the glory and the impress of his hypostasis, and bearing all things by the word of his power, having made cleansing of sins sat at the right of the Majesty on high, having become so much better than the angels as he has inherited a more different name than they.” The radiance of the glory, the impress of the hypostasis of God and Father—that is, the Only-begotten Son from him by nature—in what manner, having made cleansing of our sins (clearly through his own blood), has sat at the Father’s right and is said to have become better than the angels, though by nature and by deity’s superiority he conquers all things? Therefore even having become human he has excelled as God the invisible creation, being the same radiance and impress and having worked the cleansing of our sins by his own blood. So there is one Christ and Son and Lord.

“For both the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one; for which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: I will announce your name to my brothers.” What is holy by nature is not sanctified, because it does not need sanctification; but what has become holy as by participation from another cannot sanctify others. How then the same one sanctifies and is sanctified must be asked. He sanctifies, then, as God, having received as a property of his own nature the power to sanctify, and he is sanctified with us according to the human. So there is one Christ and Son and Lord, sanctifying divinely and being sanctified with us humanly.
